From Fig. 3b, the corresponding diffraction pattern of Fig. 3a is in accordance with B2 parent phase taken from [001] zone.

High resolution electron microscopy (HREM) image of Ti-Ni matrix in the 1Co sample annealed at 550 °C shows that very thin platelets lie on {001} plane of B2 parent phase and platelet zones consist of a few layers of atomic planes (Fig. 3c). It might be concluded that the earlier stage of the precipitation, called GP zones, produces strain contrast and diffraction streaks.
It can be seen from Fig. 3d that the uniformly dispersed precipitates are distributed in the Ti-Ni matrix. The estimated diameter of the spherical precipitates is about 5 nm as shown in Fig. 3e.
Fig. 3f shows clustered precipitation become dominant when the annealing temperature increases to 750 °C. The size of the precipitates has increased up to 50 nm.

The strong diffraction streaks can be observed in the 2Co sample likewise. And the relative intensity of diffraction streaks increases somewhat (Fig. 4a), indicating the increased size and amount of GP zones.

Fig. 4b shows the microstructure of the 2Co sample annealed at 650 °C, in which very fine spherical Ti2Co precipitates are homogeneously and densely distributed. The estimated average diameter of Ti2Co precipitates appears to be approximately 10 nm.
Fig. 4c shows the same clustered precipitation in the 2Co sample annealed at 750 °C and the size of the precipitates further increases.

For the 4Co sample annealed at 550 °C, fine and dispersed precipitates are distributed in the grain interiors and boundaries (Fig. 5a). The estimated average diameter of precipitate is approximately 15 nm.
Subsequently, It should be noted that the precipitates begin to aggregate and coarsen in the 4Co sample at annealing temperature of 650 °C (Fig. 5d).
With the annealing temperature increasing, the size of the precipitates increases up to about 150 nm as shown in Fig. 5e.
after heating treatment at 550 °C, the 0.5Co sample shows yield strength of 362 MPa and critical stress for SIM of 158 MPa.
When the content of Co increases to 1 at.%, the obvious improvement of yield strength and critical stress for SIM is up to 483 MPa and 267 MPa, respectively.
The 2Co sample annealed at 550 °C show the highest yield strength of 520 MPa and the highest critical stress for SIM of 280 MPa.

With the further increase of Co content, the yield strength of the 4Co sample decreases to 491 MPa.
yet the recovery stress first increases and then decreases with the increase of the pre-strain. The sample with the pre-strain of 8% can obtain the highest recovery stress of 482 MPa.
The Ti 44.5Ni44.5Nb9Co2 alloy annealed at 550 °C exhibits the largest completely recovery strain of 6% and the highest recovery stress of 482 MPa.
The maximal reversible recovery strain of this sample can reach 6%, which exceeds the maximal recovery strain of 4.6% in the previous Ti-Ni-Nb alloys [30].

In the light of microstructure observation, the improvement of yield strength is ascribed to the presence of coherent Ti2Co precipitates.
After annealing 550 °C for 2 h, dispersed and coherent GP zones produce higher resistance to obstruct the movement of dislocations in the 2Co sample.

Fine semi-coherent Ti2Co precipitates in 4Co sample can considerably relax strain field via the misfit in the interface. Consequently, the strengthening effect seems to be not so high as that of the coherent GP zones.
